item.title: Essays on Market Design, Complementarities, and Technology Adoption
item.description:
Monday, July 20, 2026 at 3 PM

Location: Kraft

  Speaker: Jingyun Huang Doctoral Candidate Thesis Defense Department: Economics This dissertation studies how allocation is shaped by complementarities, participation frictions, and the design of market institutions. The chapters examine settings in which agents make choices over related objects or technologies: highway contracts sold sequentially within a day, spectrum licenses sold through a simultaneous clock auction, and consumer-facing generative AI tools adopted across countries. Across these settings, the dissertation asks how observed choices reveal economic primitives, and how market outcomes change when agents face constraints on entry, capacity, information, or access. The first chapter studies sequential highway procurement auctions in Oklahoma. Morning and afternoon contracts are sold on the same day, allowing early awards to affect later entry and bidding. I estimate a structural model that separates standalone costs, cost synergies, fixed entry costs, and firm-day capacity constraints. The estimates show that small firms obtain larger proportional cost savings from same-day project synergies, but higher participation barriers limit their ability to act on these gains. Counterfactuals comparing sequential auctions, simultaneous unbundled auctions, and targeted bundling show that auction format affects both procurement spending and the distribution of awards across firms. The second chapter studies FCC Auction 110, a 5G spectrum auction in which bidders may value combinations of geographic markets. I use a revealed-preference approach to construct moment inequalities from clock-phase bidding choices and recover bounds on standalone values and geographic complementarities. The estimates support positive complementarities across markets. Counterfactual reallocations indicate that locally supported changes can raise value, though the welfare conclusions remain bounded rather than point identified. The third chapter measures global adoption of consumer-facing generative AI tools using high-frequency website traffic data from Semrush. The chapter documents rapid entry, persistent ChatGPT dominance, accelerating usage, widening adoption gaps between high- and low-income countries, and strong home-market advantages for non-U.S. tools. Together, the chapters show that allocation in modern markets depends not only on preferences and costs, but also on the institutional and technological conditions that determine who can act on them.  https://riceuniversity.zoom.us/j/3813885532?pwd=OGhoVU1aVnRCR2k5STZXTk5CZzFlZz09&omn=95611363587 (https://riceuniversity.zoom.us/j/3813885532?pwd=OGhoVU1aVnRCR2k5STZXTk5CZzFlZz09&omn=95611363587) (Department : Economics)

item.title: VEGA: A Computational Theory of Visual Grouping
item.description:
Tuesday, July 21, 2026 at 8 PM

Location: Kraft Hall

  Speaker: Shrreya Aagarwal Doctoral Candidate Thesis Defense Department: Psychology Location: Kraft Hall 110 Information organization is fundamental to how humans interact with and perceive the world. Understanding how humans naturally group interface elements is therefore essential for designing intuitive user experiences; effective grouping helps users find information more efficiently, reducing search time and frustration. Previous work in this domain has either prioritized proximity or tested Gestalt principles in isolation–this work builds a grouping hierarchy from the ground up by pitting principles directly against one another. The present work focuses on understanding users' preferred grouping (rows, columns, or neutral) when Gestalt principles compete, in order to inform a computational model of visual grouping. A series of experiments tested the effects of and interactions between various Gestalt principles through stimuli arranged in grids that were incrementally manipulated. The experiments reveal a hierarchical nature among the principles: shape similarity and common region emerge as the strongest grouping cues, followed by alignment, with proximity as the weakest. These findings challenge the proximity-first assumptions that have dominated the literature and provide key insights into the mechanisms underlying perceptual grouping. Building on these findings, this research guides the successful development of a computational model capable of predicting users' grouping preferences within a given interface. Furthermore, an additional experiment testing the model's sensitivity across various screen sizes was conducted, ensuring its generalizability to real-world contexts, such as digital ecosystems. Together, this work advances a comprehensive visual grouping theory and offers actionable principles for the design of 2-D interfaces.   (Department : Psychology)

item.title: Strange Orientations: Forrest Bess and the Texas Gulf Coast
item.description:
Thursday, July 23, 2026 at 2 PM

Location: See Zoom Link

  Speaker: Corey Stout Doctoral Candidate Thesis Defense Department: Art History In this dissertation, I explore the significance and impact of the Gulf Coast on the work of Texas artist Forrest Bess (1911-1977). Bess, represented by Betty Parsons Gallery in the 1950s and 1960s, moved to the coast to explore visions he had been having since childhood. Although art historians have acknowledged the imagery of the coastal landscape in his paintings, scholarship on Bess has largely centered on his visions and their symbolic meanings. This emphasis has obscured the formative role of the coastal environment, and I argue that the coast was not simply the setting for his exploration of these visions but was a material and conceptual context that shaped his practice. Drawing on his artworks, photographs, correspondence, and archival materials, I demonstrate how his practice emerged through a reciprocal relationship between the body and the coastal environment to produce a queer way of inhabiting space that dissolves the boundaries between the two. I first examine how Bess used modernist abstraction to produce a visual language that folded the body and coastal landscape into one another to explore queer embodiment and subjectivity. I then consider how the material and spatial conditions of the Gulf Coast expanded Bess's practice beyond the canvas to explore architecture, photography, labor, and everyday life as sites of artistic production. Finally, I show that Bess engaged with petroleum and the oil industry along the Texas Gulf Coast as a material framework for understanding the intersection of queerness and madness. By repositioning Bess within the context of the Texas Gulf Coast, I expand our understanding of his artistic practice beyond painting, while also demonstrating how Bess anticipated later developments of performance, conceptual, and environmental art.   https://riceuniversity.zoom.us/j/2066552633?pwd=KzNsbTRwM0FQQWQrWFFUMXdUMjJRZz09 (Department : Art History)

item.title: Characterization of Young Active Stars for Identifying the Youngest Exoplanets
item.description:
Thursday, July 23, 2026 at 7 PM

Location: Brockman Hall for Physics

  Speaker: Shih-Yun Tang Doctoral Candidate Thesis Defense Department: Physics & Astronomy Location: Brockman Hall for Physics 300 The most direct way to understand planet formation is to study planetary systems in their earliest evolutionary stages. As pre-main-sequence solar analogs, T Tauri stars (TTSs) are captured before and after the epoch of protoplanetary disk dispersal, marking the boundary at which the main planetary migration occurs. However, the intense magnetic activity inherent in these young hosts poses severe challenges for current detection techniques, such as the transit and radial velocity (RV) methods. Strong, localized magnetic fields suppress convective flux across the stellar photosphere, creating extensive starspots that not only contaminate true planetary signals but also introduce substantial biases when characterizing the fundamental parameters of the host stars. Without a robust means to disentangle and characterize these activity signatures, deriving reliable physical parameters necessary to infer planetary properties and constrain planet-formation models remains challenging.   This dissertation is dedicated to developing a model to simulate the effects of starspots on high-resolution stellar spectra and exploring their resulting impacts on key observational diagnostics, including RVs, photometry, and temperature-sensitive spectral lines. The thesis is organized into four primary parts. First, we analyze a young binary system, DI Tau, to demonstrate how magnetic activity compromises our ability to obtain reliable stellar parameters. Second, we calibrate and characterize a set of temperature-sensitive lines in the $H$ band to track short-term and seasonal variations in the apparent effective temperature of active TTSs. Third, we provide a comprehensive description of the development and verification of EXSPLOSYN, a grid-integrated, high-resolution spotted spectral synthesis framework. Finally, we leverage this simulation to forward-model the surface-temperature inhomogeneities of the weak-lined TTS LkCa 4 and found wavelength-dependent agreement between our simulated profiles and empirical datasets, confirming the reported differences in sensitivity to the hot and cool components at different wavelengths. With EXSPLOSYN, we also provided a critical benchmark for the widely used two-template spectral-fitting technique. We found a potential bias in the technique in overestimating spot size by a factor of 2. https://riceuniversity.zoom.us/j/92151775597?pwd=o0f7BaKC8rAFtoJTmOjaNZxzwEnk7G.1 (Department : Physics & Astronomy)

The DW Art + Climate Partners support and advise on climate programming and future projects. DiverseWorks’ Art + Climate program began in 2023-24 and consists of a climate action plan that guides the organization; programming that increases awareness of the effects of climate change; support for artists to develop environmentally sustainable practices; and the development of a new, climate-forward facility for artists, community members, and other non-profit organizations to share. Speaker BioEmily Johnson is a Bessie Award-winning choreographer, Guggenheim, Native Arts and Cultures Foundation, and United States Artists Fellow, and recipient of the Doris Duke Artist Award. She is based in Lenapehoking / New York City. Emily is of the Yup’ik Nation, and since 1998 has created work that considers the experience of sensing and seeing performance. Her dances function as portals and care processions, they engage audienceship within and through space, time, and environment — interacting with a place’s architecture, peoples, history and role in building futures. Emily is trying to make a world where performance is part of life; where performance is an integral part of our connection to each other, our environment, our stories, our past, present and future. Her choreography and gatherings have been presented across what is currently called the United States and Australia. Her large-scale project, Then a Cunning Voice and A Night We Spend Gazing at Stars is an all-night outdoor performance gathering taking place amongst 84 community-hand-made quilts. It premiered in Lenapehoking (NYC) in 2017, and was presented in Zhigaagoong (Chicago) in 2019. She choreographed the Santa Fe Opera production of Doctor Atomic, directed by Peter Sellars in 2018. Being Future Being, premiered on Tongva Land in Los Angeles in 2022. In 2011, DiverseWorks presented her performance The Thank-You Bar in conjunction with the exhibition This is Displacement: Native Artists Consider the Relationship Between Land and Identity (co-curated by Johnson and Diné visual artist Carolyn Lee Anderson).  Emily’s writing has been published and commissioned by The Open Society University Network’s Center for Human Rights and the Arts, ArtsLink Australia, unMagazine, Dance Research Journal (University of Cambridge Press); SFMOMA; Transmotion Journal, University of Kent; Movement Research Journal; Pew Center for Arts and Heritage; and the compilation Imagined Theaters: Writing for a Theoretical Stage (Routledge). Emily hosts monthly ceremonial fires on Mannahatta in partnership with Abrons Arts Center and Kai Recollet. She was the Pueblo Opera Cultural Council Diplomat at Santa Fe Opera 2018-2020, and a lead organizer of First Nations Dialogues. She was a co-compiler of the documents, Creating New Futures: Guidelines for Ethics and Equity in the Performing Arts and Notes for Equitable Funding, was a member of Creative Time’s inaugural Think Tank, and serves as a working consortium member for First Nations Performing Arts.

item.title: Ionospheric O⁺ Transport to the Inner Magnetosphere: A Global MHD and Test-Particle Study
item.description:
Wednesday, July 29, 2026 at 7 PM

Location: Herman Brown Hall

  Speaker: Yiwen Zhu Doctoral Candidate Thesis Defense Department: Physics & Astronomy Location: Herman Brown Hall HBH 254 During geomagnetic storms, ionospheric oxygen (O⁺) can become a significant constituent of Earth's inner magnetosphere, whose storm-time particle buildup drives the main-phase depression of the surface magnetic field. The ionosphere supplies this oxygen from two main regions: the dayside polar cusp and the nightside auroral oval. Their relative contribution to the inner magnetosphere, and how each population is energized as it moves inward, remain poorly quantified, in part because the transport spans scales that no single model resolves. In this thesis, we follow ionospheric oxygen from both sources to the inner magnetosphere using a global magnetohydrodynamic simulation (GAMERA/MAGE) coupled one-way to a test-particle tracer (CHIMP). Because MAGE couples models spanning a range of scales and regions, it resolves both the mesoscale bursty bulk flows (BBFs) of the plasma sheet that drive earthward transport and the particle dynamics of the inner magnetosphere. For a real storm, we compare how cusp and nightside-auroral oxygen reach the plasma sheet and the inner magnetosphere. Within an adiabatic (guiding-center) framework, we decompose the energy gain along the transport into its Fermi, betatron, and E×B contributions and quantify each, and we characterize where the oxygen departs from adiabatic behavior. The two sources follow different paths: cusp oxygen takes the long route through the lobe, while auroral oxygen enters the closed plasma sheet more directly. We also identify a drop-down channel, in which mesoscale plasma-sheet flows pull cusp oxygen down to the equatorial plasma sheet and let it enter the inner magnetosphere more efficiently. To place the contribution on a quantitative footing, we weight the test particles by O⁺ outflow fluences computed directly from the simulation's MHD variables, include charge-exchange loss, and compare the modeled oxygen against Van Allen Probes observations. Cusp oxygen enters the inner magnetosphere at higher energy and auroral oxygen at lower energy, so their relative contribution depends on the number density of ions each source delivers. Through two different storms, we show two cases in which the delivered numbers differ, giving different relative and absolute contributions of the two sources to the inner magnetosphere. Finally, we return to the cusp itself. Predicting where the cusp lies from the upstream solar wind is operationally useful. We develop a machine-learning model, gradient-boosted decision trees trained on DMSP spacecraft cusp crossings, that predicts the cusp location from solar-wind and interplanetary-magnetic-field conditions, offering a fast alternative to a full simulation. Together, these chapters connect the ionospheric sources of inner-magnetosphere oxygen to its delivery and energization: how cusp and auroral O⁺ reach the inner magnetosphere, how each is energized along the way, and how much each contributes across storms. The cusp machine-learning model complements this with a fast predictor of the cusp location from the upstream solar wind. item.title: Jesus Benavente: NUESTROWORLD
item.description:
Thursday, August 13, 2026 at 12 AM

Location: DiverseWorks, @ 5601 B Navigation Blvd & Various Locations, 5601 B Navigation Blvd, Houston, TX, 77011, United States

Jesus Benavente, A life, A Home and A Horse Named Triste, 2021, courtesy of the artist. Opening Thursday, August 13, 2026 | 6 – 8 PM Gallery Hours: Thurs – Sat 12 – 6 PM NUESTROWORLD is a satirical solo exhibition by Brooklyn-based artist Jesus Benavente, conceived of as a visual album and immersive “amusement park.” This project features interconnected works unfolding across the gallery and city, collectively highlighting Houston’s cyclical history of ambition, folly, and heartbreak. The title NUESTROWORLD is a play on Astroworld and uses Spanglish to create the phrase “The World Is Ours.” The project draws inspiration from popular events that mark specific eras of Houston’s history, such as the opening of the world-famous Astrodome and Astroworld Park in the late 60’s, Selena’s iconic Rodeo performances in the 90’s, and the folklore surrounding the 1836 capture of Santa Anna during the Battle of San Jacinto as part of the Texas Revolution. Together, they build a story, a world developed over time that underscores sacrifice, instills resilience, and highlights a Texas attitude of “come and take it.”  ARTIST BIO: Jesus Benavente is a visual artist based in Brooklyn, New York. Jesus earned an MFA from Rutgers University and attended Skowhegan School of Painting and Sculpture. Recent exhibitions and performances include the Whitney Museum of American Art, New York; Queens Museum, Queens; LTD Los Angeles, Los Angeles; Performa 13, New York; Acre Projects, Chicago; Chinati Foundation, Marfa; the Neuberger Museum of Art, Purchase, NY; Shin Museum of Art, South Korea; Vox Populi, Philadelphia; Socrates Sculpture Park, New York; and Austin Museum of Art. Benavente was born in San Antonio, Texas.

item.title: SynthX "Unlocking the Clinical Potential of Chemical Innovation" Workshop
item.description:
Tuesday, September 8, 2026 at 5 PM

Location: BioScience Research Collaborative

By harnessing the expertise and resources of various groups within the TMC, this long-term series aims to bridge the gap between biomedical innovations and clinical applications, offering valuable insights to researchers from Rice and the TMC regarding biomedical challenges and potential solutions. Faculty, postdocs, students, and other researchers are invited to attend. Lunch is provided. — Prof. Lingyan Shi and her team are developing and applying new ultrafast laser scanning multimodal imaging and spectroscopic technologies, such as stimulated Raman scattering (SRS), DO-SRS, second harmonic generation (SHG), Fluorescence Lifetime Imaigng (FLIM), and multiphoton fluorescence (MPF) microscopy, for visualizing molecular events and metabolic dynamics in situ at subcellular resolution for studying aging and diseases. Prof. Shi and her team discovered "Golden Window" (from 1550nm to 1870nm) wavelength for deep optical tissue imaging (Shi et al., 2016), established PRM (Zhang et al., 2024) SRS and A-POD (Jang et al., 2023) super resolution multi-molecular imaging platform. Shi Lab is developing and applying bioorthogonal SRS imaging methods for dissecting complex cellular machinery in living organisms during aging processes and disease progression, offering powerful tools potentially for diagnosis, assessing therapeutic efficacy/resistance, as well as for mechanistic understanding of scientific fundamentals in neurodegenerative diseases, cancer, drug discovery, and aging processes.

item.description:
Saturday, October 3, 2026 at 12 AM

Location: DiverseWorks – Gallery @ MATCH, 3400 Main Street, Houston, TX, 77002, United States

October 3-24, 2026DiverseWorks Gallery @ MATCHGallery Hours: 12 noon – 6 pm, Thursday-Saturday Celebrated for her large-scale social choreographies, Emily Johnson / Catalyst’s newest project, Overflow Radio is a performance, skill-share, planting of 1000 trees, and radio transmission from across territories. In conjunction with the world premiere of Overflow Radio in Mni Sóta Makoce (Minneapolis), DiverseWorks hosts an Overflow Radio: Šakotayišol Nunuš Constellation here in Houston. Over 24 non-consecutive hours, we will gather in-person to listen to twelve First Nations and Indigenous authors, poets, and scholars live-broadcasting from their home territories and First Nations. We’ll pay attention to other scales, other forms, other knowledges. We’ll traverse together, transcending colonial borders, languages and time. We’ll feast and celebrate the making of community, as we practice our shared commitment to creating our possible futures, as we gather what we need to know. The program is developed in collaboration with Emily Johnson and local Indigenous and Native artists to include talks, skill-shares, listening gatherings, an exhibition, and performances by Aveda Adara, Chiara Beaumont, ChiChi, Karen Navarro, Aryn Ward and Monica Villarreal, with additional participating artists and community partners to be announced. The project is co-organized by DiverseWorks, Emily Johnson / Catalyst and the participating artists and partners. item.title: Across Two Seas Symposium
item.description:
Thursday, October 8, 2026 at 10 AM

Location: Moody Center

Across Two Seas brings together scholars, curators, artists, and community members for a multi-day symposium at Rice University on Black subjectivities across the medieval and early modern Mediterranean, Islamic world, and Indian Ocean. Through panels, film screenings, public conversations, and interdisciplinary dialogue, the symposium explores how Black subjects were represented in artistic, literary, and documentary sources and how these representations were shaped by trade, travel, religion, knowledge-making, and cultural exchange. By connecting Europe, North Africa, the Arabian Peninsula, East Africa, India, and Southeast Asia, Across Two Seas expands the geography of premodern race studies and places the Indian Ocean at the center of conversations too often framed primarily through Europe. The symposium invites broader publics to consider how histories of Blackness were made across multiple regions, media, and worlds.
